title: Windows support: the transport abstraction is the gate
description:
README:84 promises a Windows named pipe at \\.\pipe\persona-workload-{sid}, README:90 promises EXE-signing consumer attestation, and the attestor table lists Windows for Tailscale, FIDO2 and Windows Hello. None of it exists, there is no Windows CI leg, and the code is structurally Unix-only.

Measured on this tree:
  21 sites   UnixListener / UnixStream        -> named pipes
   4 sites   libc::getuid                     -> SID
   4 sites   SO_PEERCRED                      -> GetNamedPipeClientProcessId
   1 site    tokio::signal::unix              -> ctrl_c or service control handler
   2 files   tailscale.rs, ssh.rs assume unix sockets
Exactly one #[cfg(not(unix))] exists in the whole workspace.

The 21 transport sites are the gate. Nothing else can be attempted until the listener and stream are an abstraction rather than a concrete tokio::net::Unix* type, because the socket path, consumer attestation and the daemon's accept loop all bottom out there. hire-grpc/src/socket.rs already carries the ponytail comment saying so: 'unix domain sockets only | ceiling: Windows needs a named pipe, which this function cannot express | upgrade path: abstract the transport over UnixListener/UnixStream first, then return a platform-tagged endpoint instead of a PathBuf'.

The good news, and where to start: hire-core is ALREADY portable. Zero files reference std::os::unix, libc, or unix sockets, and its dependencies (thiserror, serde, hkdf, sha2, ring, x509-cert, jsonwebtoken, serde_json) all build on Windows. That crate holds the crypto, the HKDF pseudonym derivation, the SPIFFE ID types and the signer.

Suggested order:
  1. Windows CI leg for hire-core only, to lock in the portability that exists.
  2. Abstract the transport.
  3. Then named pipe path, Windows consumer attestation, signal handling.
  4. Then decide whether Windows Hello is an attestor worth writing.
